Solution 3 has the correct final answer, c = 3.

The refinement must agree with the known bound n ≤ 2m − 3 at k = 3, which forces ⌊(3+c)/2⌋ = 3, so c ∈ {3, 4}. Solution 2's c = 2 gives 2m − 2 at k = 3, which is weaker than 2m − 3, so it cannot be a refinement. Solution 1's c = 1 fails the same test.

To pin down c = 3 rather than 4, use the rank-metric Singleton bound. Solution 3 derives d ≥ n − m + 2 from the intersecting property, which gives km ≤ n(2m − n − 1). Writing n = 2m − j, this forces k ≲ 2(j − 1), so j ≥ ⌈k/2⌉ + 1 = ⌊(k+3)/2⌋. Hence n ≤ 2m − ⌊(k+3)/2⌋, which is c = 3. I checked the algebra and it is consistent; I did not verify the geometric step (the line/point dimension inequality) or the sharpness claim against the source paper.
